pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (ages 11-13) children move from calculating a single mean to DESCRIBING and COMPARING whole distributions: computing mean, median, mode and range, choosing which average best represents a data set, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure. Two ideas carry the teaching, and both are about judgement rather than calculation. First, the three averages are not interchangeable: the mean is influenced by every value (so a single outlier drags it), while the median is robust and stays representative when the data is skewed — so the CHOICE of average must fit the shape of the data. Second, an average alone does not describe a distribution: comparing two data sets requires a measure of CENTRE and a measure of SPREAD (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ wildly in variability. The characteristic errors are reporting the mean regardless of skew, treating the outlier as affecting all averages equally (or deleting it unthinkingly), and comparing sets on the mean alone while ignoring spread.
bestPractices: Compute all three averages on the SAME data set (especially a skewed one or one with an outlier) so children see them diverge and can discuss which best represents a typical value
Make the outlier's differential effect explicit: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier — the mean chases it, the median barely moves — so 'robust' has a concrete meaning
Teach that describing a distribution needs CENTRE and SPREAD together; compare two data sets on an average AND the range, and show two sets with equal means but different spreads
Tie the choice of average to the data's shape: median for skewed data or data with an outlier, mode for categorical / most-common questions, mean for roughly symmetric numerical data
Insist the range is a single number (highest minus lowest), a measure of spread — not the two extreme values
Draw conclusions in context ('Class A did better on average but was less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not just calculated
keyRepresentations: A data set shown on a number line with mean and median both marked, and an outlier that can be added/removed to see each measure respond
Side-by-side dot plots of two data sets with the same mean but different spreads (centre vs spread made visible)
A skewed distribution where mean, median and mode fall in visibly different places
The range shown as a labelled distance from lowest to highest value
commonMisconceptions: Reporting the mean as 'the average' regardless of skew or outliers, when the median would better represent a typical value
Thinking an outlier affects the mean and median equally, or deleting an outlier without justification, rather than seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
Comparing two data sets on their averages alone and ignoring the spread (a frequent error is to ignore variability entirely)
Giving the range as the two extreme values rather than their difference; or situating the mean at the centre of the range even when the data is skewed

learn.summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) move from calculating a single mean to describing and comparing whole distributions of one variable: computing mean, median, mode and range, judging which average best represents a data set given its shape, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure differently. Two judgements carry the topic: (1) the three averages are not interchangeable — the mean is pulled by every value (so an outlier drags it) while the median is robust, so the choice of average must fit the data's shape; and (2) an average alone does not describe a distribution — comparing two sets needs a measure of centre AND a measure of spread (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ widely in variability.

activities.title: Watch the averages diverge: move a value far out
feedback: If the learner says the median moved as much as the mean, have them recount the ordered values: the middle position stays near the cluster, whereas the sum rises by how far the value was moved, so the mean shifts by that amount divided by the number of values — a change the median does not share.

If the learner deletes the far-out value without justification, ask what real reason (e.g. a recording error versus a genuine value) would justify removing it, and show what each average does when it is kept.
If the learner reports the pulled-up mean as 'the typical score', point to the cluster and ask whether that mean sits among most of the data.
activities.rationale: Computing all three averages on a clustered set and recomputing them after one value is moved far out lets learners see the measures diverge, giving 'the mean is pulled by outliers, the median is robust' a concrete meaning rather than being a slogan. Moving an existing point (rather than adding one) keeps the count fixed so the median's stability is clearly attributable to order statistics.
sourceClaims: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Start with a small set of values on a stated scale (for example reaction times in whole seconds, or scores out of 40) clustered around 4-5, and compute the mean, median, mode and range by hand.
Record all four measures, then take ONE of those values and move it far out to a value the scale allows (for example 30), keeping the number of data points the same.
Recompute the mean and median with the far-out value, and compare each to its value before.
State in words which measure moved a lot and which barely moved, and explain why the mean was dragged while the median held.

If a draggable dot plot with mean, median, mode and range read out live is available, drag one point far from the cluster and watch the mean line chase it while the median stays put or moves at most to a neighbouring value in the cluster (for example, if the dragged point crosses from below the middle to above it) — this makes the differential effect visible in real time.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it a lot; the median, based on order/position, is robust and barely moves. 'Robust' becomes concrete when you see the two measures respond differently to the same far-out value.

activities.title: Same mean, different spread: why centre is not enough
feedback: If the learner concludes the sets are 'the same' from equal means, show the two ranges side by side and ask which class has students scoring far from the average.
If the learner lists the two extreme values instead of the range, ask for the single distance between them (highest − lowest).
If the learner reports only the range and forgets the centre, point out that spread without a centre also fails to describe the data.
activities.rationale: Describing and comparing distributions needs centre and spread together; comparing on an average alone is a frequent error, so building the comparison from both measures targets that gap directly.
sourceClaims: A frequent error is to ignore the spread of data; the intuitive notion of variability concerns how much values differ from each other, and different words (variation, dispersion, spread) are open to different interpretations — so describing data needs an explicit measure of spread

KS3 pupils describe, interpret and compare observed distributions of a single variable through appropriate measures of central tendency (mean, mode, median) and spread (range), including consideration of outliers
learnerActions: Take two data sets (for example two classes' test scores) that have the same mean but clearly different spreads.
Compute the mean and the range (highest minus lowest, a single number) for each set.
Decide whether 'same mean' means the classes performed identically, and justify the answer using the ranges.
Write a conclusion in context that mentions BOTH centre and spread, e.g. 'Both classes scored about the same on average, but Class A was far more consistent.'
If side-by-side dot plots with adjustable spreads at a fixed mean are available, line the two plots up and compare how wide each is while the mean stays equal.
activities.intendedInsight: An average alone does not describe a distribution. Two sets with equal means can differ widely in variability, so a fair comparison reports a measure of centre AND a measure of spread.

activities.title: Which average would you report, and why?
feedback: If the learner defaults to the mean on a skewed set, ask whether that mean sits among most of the values or is pulled toward the tail.
If the learner assumes the mean is always central, have them locate the mean and the bulk of the data on the skewed set and compare.
If the learner picks the mode where values are all distinct numerical measurements, ask whether 'most common' is meaningful here.
activities.rationale: Tying the choice of average to the data's shape confronts the fragmented notions of 'average' and the characteristic error of reporting the mean regardless of skew.
sourceClaims: Students' notions of 'average' fragment into most-frequent-value/mode, reasonable value, midpoint and algorithmic relationship — each true in some circumstances but not others — so which average is appropriate depends on the data

The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Given a skewed data set (or one with an outlier), compute mean, median and mode and note where each falls.
Choose which average best represents a typical value and write a one-sentence justification tied to the data's shape.
For a most-common / categorical question, decide whether the mode is the right choice and say why.
Check a tempting claim such as 'the mean always sits in the middle of the range' against your skewed data and explain whether it holds.
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate average depends on the data: the median represents a typical value better for skewed data or data with an outlier; the mode suits most-common / categorical questions; the mean suits roughly symmetric numerical data. Learners' informal notions of 'average' (most frequent, reasonable value, midpoint, algorithm) are each true only in some circumstances.

activities.title: Compute-and-justify checks
feedback: If a comparison answer mentions only averages, prompt: 'What about how spread out each set is?'
If the range is given as two values, require the single difference.
If the learner says the mean and median change equally when the outlier is removed, have them actually recompute both.
activities.rationale: Short scorable items using data sets where the averages genuinely diverge give a check that can catch report-the-mean-regardless and ignore-the-spread errors. Such items verify both procedure and judgement but do not by themselves build the underlying reasoning, which the manipulation and comparison activities develop.
learnerActions: Compute mean, median, mode and range for a given set, stating the range as one number (highest − lowest).
For a skewed set, pick which average best represents it and give the reason.
For two sets, write a conclusion that cites BOTH an average AND the range, so a centre-only comparison is marked incomplete.
For an outlier item, state which of the mean or median changes more when the outlier is removed, and by roughly how much.

Optional: a usable worked set is sleep hours 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 (mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7), where the outlier 2 pulls the mean DOWN below the cluster — note this direction is opposite to an upward-pulling outlier, and the median stays representative.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct computation plus correct judgement (choice of average, differential outlier effect, centre-and-spread comparison) are both required; getting the arithmetic right is not the same as reasoning about the distribution.

constraints: Use data sets where the three averages genuinely diverge (skewed data or a clear outlier); on near-symmetric data the point about choosing the right average is invisible.
State the measurement context/scale for any example so the outlier is a plausible value on that scale (not off-scale), and match the direction of pull (up or down) to the data.
State the range as a single number (highest − lowest), a measure of spread, not the pair of extreme values.
Always draw conclusions in context (e.g. 'better on average but less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not merely calculated.

A fixed annotated distribution can mark where mean, median and mode fall and label the range as a distance, and is useful as a reference or worked example; because its data cannot be moved, pair it with an activity where learners change the data and watch the measures respond.

Scorable compute-and-justify items can assess both procedure and judgement and can be used during teaching, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning that choosing an average and comparing distributions require; include construction and explanation.

An in-role 'data analyst' who argues a naive claim ('same mean, so the classes are identical') for the learner to challenge can surface and sharpen reasoning; use it as a follow-on once learners have manipulated or computed the measures, since dialogue alone does not show the measures changing.
Removing an outlier must be justified by a reason (e.g. a recording error), not done reflexively to tidy the data.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed a live manipulable tool achieves what 'calculation alone cannot', that a static image 'cannot' teach the core idea, and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordances/limits (manipulation makes the differential effect visible; a fixed image serves as reference; single-variable data is one-dimensional so an extra spatial axis is not needed here).

The outlier direction differs between the upward illustration (moving a value to 30) and the original diagnostic (sleep value 2 pulling the mean DOWN). Both are valid; facilitators should ensure the chosen direction matches the data so learners see the correct direction of pull. The concrete sleep dataset (7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2; mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7) from the original diagnostic is retained as an optional worked example.

Activity 1 was adjusted to MOVE an existing value far out (count fixed) rather than ADD a value, so the median's robustness is clearly due to order statistics and not to a change in the number of data points. Feedback was corrected so the mean's sensitivity is stated accurately: the sum changes by the displacement and the mean by that displacement divided by the number of values, not by the 'full size' of the value.
Source claims were retained only where they directly support an activity's teaching principle; the fourth activity cites none because no source establishes efficacy of scorable items.
Legacy confidence was 'high'; this has not been independently re-validated here.

probeDeeper: 'The mean is about 7 but one person slept only 2 hours — which number better describes a typical night, and why?' — pushes the skew/outlier → median reasoning into words
'What happens to the mean and to the median if I remove the 2? Which changes more?' — tests the differential effect directly
Counterexample: 'Both classes have a mean of 60 — does that mean they did equally well? What else would you check?' — forces spread into the comparison
'When would the MODE be the best average to report?' — probes appropriateness of measure on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: computes mean, median, mode and range correctly (range = highest − lowest, one number); recognises the 2 as an outlier that drags the MEAN down while the MEDIAN stays representative, and reports the median as the typical value with that reason; and when comparing the two classes uses BOTH an average AND the range/spread ('similar on average but Class A is more consistent'), not the average alone. Seeing the outlier's differential effect and comparing on centre AND spread are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Outlier treated as affecting all averages equally, or reported mean regardless of the outlier — not seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the mean prerequisite: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier so the child sees the mean chase it while the median holds; the mean is influenced by every value, the median is not
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On tasks (1)-(2) the child reports the mean as the typical value despite the 2 pulling it below the cluster, or claims the median is affected as much as the mean, or deletes the 2 without justification

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares two data sets on the average alone, ignoring the spread — concludes two sets with similar means are 'the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: show two sets with equal means but very different ranges and ask 'are these really the same?'; describing a distribution needs centre AND spread
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child bases the conclusion only on the means and does not mention the range/spread, missing that one class is far more variable

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong average for the data's shape — uses the mean for skewed data (or thinks the mean always sits in the middle of the range) rather than the more representative median/mode
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the choice to the shape: for skewed data or data with an outlier the median represents a typical value better; for most-common/categorical questions the mode; reteach the meaning of the measures via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child defaults to the mean without considering that the skew/outlier makes the median more representative, or expects the mean to be central regardless of shape

errorPatterns.pattern: Range as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values rather than the single number highest − lowest
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the range as one number — a distance/spread from lowest to highest — by marking both ends and computing the difference; reteach the term via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child states the range as '2 to 9' (or names lowest and highest) instead of 7

responseLevels.gap: Computes the measures unreliably or gives the range as two numbers; reports the mean regardless of an outlier; compares two sets on the mean alone
responseLevels.full: Computes all four measures, recognises and explains the outlier's differential pull on mean versus median, chooses the appropriate average for the data's shape, and compares two distributions on BOTH centre and spread — transferring the reasoning to a fresh pair of data sets
responseLevels.partial: Correctly computes mean, median, mode and range, but treats the mean as the average to report regardless of skew/outliers, or compares distributions using centre only — has the procedures without the judgement about which measure fits or that spread matters

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small data set with a clear outlier — e.g. hours of sleep: 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 — and a second pair of data sets for comparison (two classes' test scores with similar means but different spreads). Set these tasks and WATCH how they work: (1) 'Find the mean, median, mode and range of the sleep data.' (2) 'Which average best describes a typical night's sleep here? Use it.' (3) 'Compare these two classes and tell me what you can conclude.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint that the 2 is an outlier, nor that comparing needs spread as well as an average.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) forces the choice of average: a child who reports the mean regardless reveals they don't grasp that an outlier makes it unrepresentative, while a child who has the idea switches to the median and says why. Task (3) is built with similar means but different spreads, so a child comparing on the mean alone concludes 'the same' whereas a child who understands distributions cites the spread. The two separate calculation from the judgement the topic is about.
